 As Florida voters head to the polls Tuesday, one of the biggest decisions on the ballot could impact both their wallets and the communities where they live.
 Amendment 3 proposes significant changes to Florida’s property-tax system, potentially lowering taxes for many homeowners while raising concerns about how cities and counties would pay for essential services.
 Florida Amendment 3: What a yes or no vote means for homeowners and local services. CBS12's Paige Meyer reports. 
 Supporters argue the measure would provide much-needed financial relief as housing costs continue to rise. Opponents warn it could reduce funding for police protection, infrastructure and other local government services.
 The amendment needs at least 60% of the statewide vote to pass.
 What would Amendment 3 change?
 Amendment 3 would increase Florida’s homestead property-tax exemption , allowing qualifying homeowners to pay taxes on a smaller portion of their property’s assessed value.
 Under the proposal, the exemption for non-school property taxes would increase to:
 $150,000 in 2027
 $250,000 in 2028
 The exemption would then be adjusted for inflation in future years.
 Florida Amendment 3, the debate over property taxes, touches on public safety and government spending. Supporters say the proposal would make homeownership more affordable. Opponents warn that reducing property tax revenue could force communities to reconsider police protection and capital improvement projects. (WPEC) 
 The changes would apply to qualifying primary residences. School-district property taxes would not be affected.
 The proposal would also lower the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties, including certain rental and commercial properties, from 10% to 5%.
 What does a yes or no vote mean?
 Voting YES : A yes vote supports increasing the homestead exemption, potentially lowering property-tax bills for qualifying homeowners. It would also limit annual assessment increases on non-homestead properties and change certain rules governing local property-tax revenue.
 Voting NO: A no vote would reject the proposed changes and keep the existing property-tax system in place.
 How could Amendment 3 impact local communities?
 While many homeowners could see savings, the proposal has sparked concerns about its potential impact on local government budgets. Property taxes are a major source of revenue for cities and counties, helping pay for police departments, public safety, roads, infrastructure improvements and other services. 
 If homeowners pay less in property taxes, local governments could collect less revenue. That could force some municipalities to reconsider spending priorities, postpone infrastructure improvements, adjust department budgets or look for other ways to fund services.
 A Leon County judge has ruled that the ballot language for Florida's proposed property tax constitutional amendment is misleading and must be rewritten before appearing on the November ballot. (WPEC) 
 However, the amendment would not automatically require cities or counties to eliminate programs or reduce police staffing. Those decisions would depend on individual local government budgets and how officials respond to potential revenue losses. Supporters, meanwhile, argue that local governments should operate within tighter budgets and reduce unnecessary spending rather than continue placing the financial burden on homeowners. They say the proposed tax relief could help make homeownership more affordable and allow residents to keep more of their money.
 The debate ultimately centers on how to balance property-tax relief for homeowners with the funding needed to maintain local services.
 If Amendment 3 passes, the changes would begin to roll out on Jan. 1, 2027.
 What voters need to know before heading to the polls
 Polls are open Tuesday, Nov. 3, from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. across Florida.
 Voters are urged to double-check their assigned polling location before leaving home, as heavy rainfall and flooding have forced election officials to temporarily relocate several polling places across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast.
 Changes have been announced in Palm Beach, St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River and Okeechobee counties.
 In Palm Beach County, two polling locations have been relocated:
 Casa Rio Clubhouse in Riviera Beach has moved to RB Preparatory and Achievement Academy at 7071 Garden Road.
 Ironhorse Country Club in West Palm Beach has moved to North County Senior Center at 5217 Northlake Blvd. in Palm Beach Gardens.
 Additional changes have been announced in other counties, including several locations in St. Lucie County and a polling place in Martin County.
 Election officials say affected voters should report to their newly assigned locations. On Election Day, voters must cast their ballots at the polling place assigned to their precinct.
 Check your polling location before heading out: 
 Palm Beach County: https://www.votepalmbeach.gov 
 St. Lucie County: https://www.stlucievotes.gov 
 Martin County: https://www.martinvotes.gov 
 Indian River County: https://www.voteindianriver.gov 
 Okeechobee County: https://www.voteokeechobee.gov 
 Voters can also check the Florida Division of Elections website for updated information about polling-place relocations caused by flooding.
 Election officials encourage residents to allow extra travel time and verify their polling location to avoid delays on Election Day.
